content:
"The Northern Territory police are facing severe criticism in the wake of a coroner's report revealing their neglect regarding the welfare of individuals in custody. The coroner, Greg Cavanagh, highlighted a disturbing pattern of inaction by police concerning numerous self-harm and suicide attempts that occurred in caged police vehicles. This oversight particularly underscores the tragic death of a 23-year-old man last year, who was known to be vulnerable.

Cavanagh pointed out that an internal report had recommended the installation of CCTV cameras in caged vehicles back in 2013, following the death of another individual in custody. However, the police did not act on these crucial recommendations. In the three years leading up to the tragic incident, there were at least 16 documented attempts to take one’s life in these vehicles, with six instances where individuals were only discovered when they were semi-conscious or unconscious. Cavanagh's chilling remarks emphasized that it was not a matter of 'if' a death would occur in the back of a police van, but rather 'when.'

The report's revelations emerged as local law enforcement found themselves entangled in a different crisis on 16 September last year. While responding to a noise complaint in Darwin, two officers stumbled upon a serious car accident involving a Toyota Hilux that had crashed into a palm tree at a busy intersection near Darwin airport. They discovered 23-year-old Dale Scott Walkinshaw, who was unharmed but grappling with an urgent situation. He was holding a young woman, whom he had just met at a bar, in his arms. The woman, injured and drifting in and out of consciousness, had suffered a severe back injury in the accident.

Compounded by the earlier issues regarding police accountability and welfare concerns in custody, it was revealed that Walkinshaw was well over the legal limit for alcohol consumption, registering a blood alcohol level of 0.149. This incident highlights not only the systemic failures within the police force regarding vulnerable individuals in their care but also the complex challenges faced by officers on the streets as they address a myriad of public safety issues."
